questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Closed, open and isolated systems
questions.learningObjective: Classify a system by its exchanges with surroundings
questions.stem: Ticket 12 models a lake that exchanges water but not phosphorus with its surroundings; which system type fits best?

options.text: A closed system, because matter is conserved
A closed system for phosphorus, open for water
options.misconception: mixes two labels for one boundary

options.text: An isolated system, because no energy enters
options.misconception: ignores that energy exchange still occurs

options.text: An open system, because water crosses the boundary
options.misconception: confuses one exchange with full openness

questions.explanation: A closed system exchanges energy but not matter with its surroundings. The lake still receives sunlight and heat, so it is not isolated. The phosphorus stock is conserved within the chosen boundary.
questions.hint: Check both matter and energy exchanges

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Where a system boundary is drawn
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a boundary choice changes which flows count
questions.stem: Ticket 18 asks why drawing the boundary around a watershed instead of a single field changes which nutrient flows are internal.

answer.exemplar: A watershed boundary keeps rainfall and river outflow as external flows, while a field boundary treats runoff between fields as internal, so the same process changes role depending on the chosen boundary.

questions.explanation: The boundary decides what counts as a flow versus a transfer. Moving the boundary reclassifies interactions without changing the physical process, which is why results must state the boundary used.
questions.hint: State the boundary before counting flows

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Steady state against static balance
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish steady state from static equilibrium
questions.stem: Ticket 24 describes a reservoir with equal inflow and outflow but water still moving through it; what condition holds?

options.text: Static equilibrium, because levels do not change
options.misconception: confuses no net change with no motion

options.text: Closed balance, because inputs equal outputs

questions.explanation: Steady state means storage is constant while flows continue. Static equilibrium implies no movement at all, which is not true when water flows through.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Storage time from a stored amount and one flow
questions.learningObjective: Compute residence time from stock and flow
questions.stem: Ticket 31 gives a lake stock of 800 cubic metres and an outflow of 40 cubic metres per day; what is the residence time in days?
questions.explanation: Residence time equals stock divided by flow, so 800 divided by 40 gives 20 days. The result assumes the flow is the only loss and is constant.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Closed-form response of a feedback loop
questions.learningObjective: Identify the closed-form decay of a first-order loop
questions.stem: Ticket 37 models a stock that loses a fixed fraction each step; which expression describes the long-term response?

options.text: A linear decline to zero in finite steps
A sinusoidal oscillation around the mean
An exponential approach to a new steady state
A step change with no transient

questions.explanation: A first-order feedback loop produces exponential adjustment toward equilibrium. The stock changes by a fraction each step, so the response is never an abrupt step.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A reinforcing positive feedback
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a reinforcing feedback loop
questions.stem: Ticket 42 notes that thawing permafrost releases methane, which warms the climate and thaws more permafrost; what kind of loop is this?

options.text: A reinforcing loop that amplifies change
A negative feedback that stabilises temperature
options.misconception: reverses the polarity of the loop

options.text: A balancing loop with a delay
A neutral loop with no net effect

questions.explanation: The loop amplifies the initial warming, so it is reinforcing. Negative feedback would push the system back toward its starting state.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: A damping negative feedback
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a balancing feedback loop
questions.stem: Ticket 47 describes predator numbers rising when prey is abundant and falling when prey is scarce; what kind of loop is this?

options.text: A reinforcing loop that grows without bound
A neutral interaction with no effect
A damping loop that counteracts prey change

questions.explanation: Predation rises with prey and falls with prey scarcity, pushing prey back toward balance. That counteracting action is negative feedback.

options.text: No change because the factor is near one
Oscillation or overshoot around the target

questions.explanation: A correction factor above one overcorrects, so the system can overshoot and oscillate. Values below one give gentler convergence.

questions.stem: Ticket 60 estimates 2.0 gigawatts of electrical power for 86400 seconds; how many joules are produced in one day?
questions.explanation: Energy equals power times time, so 2.0e9 watts times 86400 seconds gives 1.728e14 joules. The estimate checks the scale of daily generation.

questions.topic: An atmospheric stock from a mixing ratio
questions.learningObjective: Convert a mixing ratio to a stock mass
questions.stem: Ticket 66 uses a mixing ratio of 400 ppm and an atmosphere mass of 5.15e18 kg; what is the carbon dioxide stock in kg?
questions.explanation: Stock equals mixing ratio times total mass, so 400e-6 times 5.15e18 kg gives 2.06e15 kg. The ppm is treated as a mass fraction.

questions.learningObjective: Convert an annual rate to a per-second rate
questions.stem: Ticket 72 gives an annual emission of 3.15e10 kg; what is the equivalent rate in kg per second using 3.15e7 seconds per year?
questions.explanation: Divide the annual amount by seconds per year, so 3.15e10 divided by 3.15e7 equals 1000 kg per second. The units cancel cleanly.

questions.stem: Ticket 78 adds 12 kg of pollutant to 3.0e6 litres of water each day; what is the concentration in mg per litre?
questions.explanation: 12 kg equals 12,000,000 mg, divided by 3.0e6 litres gives 4 mg per litre. The daily load and volume are assumed constant.

options.misconception: off by three orders of magnitude

questions.explanation: For water with density near 1 kg per litre, one part per million by mass is about one milligram per litre. The equality comes from the density of water.

questions.explanation: One kilowatt is 1000 joules per second and one hour is 3600 seconds, so the product is 3,600,000 joules.

questions.stem: Ticket 96 gives surface pressure of 101325 pascals; what is the mass of the air column above one square metre in kg?
questions.explanation: Mass per area equals pressure divided by gravity, so 101325 divided by 9.81 gives about 10332.6 kg per square metre. The result is the weight of the whole air column.

questions.stem: Ticket 102 has reservoir A losing 5 kg per day to reservoir B while B gains 5 kg per day; if A starts at 100 kg and B at 20 kg, what is the total mass after 10 days?
questions.explanation: No mass leaves the two-reservoir system, so the total stays 100 plus 20, or 120 kg. Internal transfer does not change the combined stock.

questions.stem: Ticket 108 drops a 2 kg mass through 5 metres; how many joules of potential energy are released using g equals 9.8?
questions.explanation: Potential energy change equals mass times gravity times height, so 2 times 9.8 times 5 gives 98 joules. Air resistance is ignored in the ticket.

questions.stem: Ticket 114 records a measured value of 98 against an accepted value of 100; what is the percent error?
questions.explanation: Percent error is the absolute difference divided by the accepted value times 100, so 2 divided by 100 times 100 gives 2 percent. The sign is dropped by convention.

questions.explanation: The complement is 0.9 cubed, or 0.729, so at least one exceedance has probability 1 minus 0.729, which is 0.271. Independence is assumed.

Yes, but only for electrical power

questions.explanation: A watt is a joule per second, and a joule is a newton metre, so the base dimensions are kg m^2 s^-3. The proposed unit matches exactly.

questions.topic: Converting an annual rate to a per-second rate
questions.learningObjective: Convert an annual rate to per second
questions.stem: Ticket 312 gives an annual rate of 6.3e10 kg; what is the per-second rate using 3.15e7 seconds per year?
questions.explanation: Divide the annual amount by seconds per year, so 6.3e10 divided by 3.15e7 equals 2000 kg per second. The units cancel cleanly.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Concentration from a daily load and a daily volume
questions.learningObjective: Compute concentration from load and volume
questions.stem: Ticket 318 adds 6 kg of pollutant to 2.0e6 litres of water each day; what is the concentration in mg per litre?
questions.explanation: 6 kg equals 6,000,000 mg, divided by 2.0e6 litres gives 3 mg per litre. The daily load and volume are assumed constant.

questions.topic: Parts per million against milligrams per litre
questions.learningObjective: Relate ppm to mg per litre
questions.stem: Ticket 324 states 2 ppm in water; what is that in mg per litre near 1 kg per litre?
questions.explanation: For water near 1 kg per litre, 1 ppm is about 1 mg per litre, so 2 ppm is about 2 mg per litre. The link comes from water density.

questions.topic: Energy unit arithmetic from a watt
questions.learningObjective: Convert kilowatt-hours to joules
questions.stem: Ticket 330 records 2 kilowatt-hours of energy; how many joules is that?
questions.explanation: Two kilowatt-hours means 2000 watts for 3600 seconds, giving 7,200,000 joules. One kilowatt-hour is 3,600,000 joules.

questions.topic: Atmospheric column mass from surface pressure
questions.learningObjective: Compute column mass from pressure
questions.stem: Ticket 336 gives surface pressure of 100000 pascals; what is the mass of the air column above one square metre in kg?
questions.explanation: Mass per area equals pressure divided by gravity, so 100000 divided by 9.81 gives about 10193.7 kg per square metre. The result is the whole air column.

questions.topic: Closing a two-reservoir mass balance
questions.learningObjective: Close a mass balance across two reservoirs
questions.stem: Ticket 342 has reservoir X at 80 kg and reservoir Y at 40 kg with 10 kg moving from X to Y; what is the total mass?
questions.explanation: Internal transfer does not change the combined stock, so the total remains 80 plus 40, or 120 kg. Only external flows change totals.

questions.subject: ENVIRONMENTAL_SCIENCE
questions.topic: Potential energy released by a falling mass
questions.learningObjective: Compute potential energy for a falling mass
questions.stem: Ticket 348 drops a 3 kg mass through 4 metres; how many joules are released using g equals 9.8?
questions.explanation: Potential energy change equals mass times gravity times height, so 3 times 9.8 times 4 gives 117.6 joules. Air resistance is ignored.
questions.hint: Use m times g times h

questions.topic: Percent error against an accepted value
questions.learningObjective: Compute percent error for a measurement
questions.stem: Ticket 354 records a measured value of 95 against an accepted value of 100; what is the percent error?
questions.explanation: Percent error is the absolute difference divided by the accepted value times 100, so 5 divided by 100 times 100 gives 5 percent. The sign is dropped.

questions.topic: Probability of at least one exceedance
questions.learningObjective: Compute probability of at least one exceedance
questions.stem: Ticket 360 assumes a 0.2 chance of exceedance each day; what is the probability of at least one in 2 independent days?
questions.explanation: The complement is 0.8 squared, or 0.64, so at least one exceedance has probability 1 minus 0.64, which is 0.36. Independence is assumed.

questions.topic: Checking a derived unit for dimension
questions.learningObjective: Check a derived unit's dimensions
questions.stem: Ticket 366 proposes measuring force as kg times metre per second squared; is this dimensionally consistent with a newton?

options.text: No, because mass should be squared
No, because time should be cubed
Yes, it matches kg m s^-2
Yes, but only for gravitational force

questions.explanation: A newton is kg m s^-2 by definition. The proposed unit matches exactly, regardless of the type of force.
